name: Metabolic Response to Injury, Surgical Stress, and Clinical Nutrition

reference.source: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22nd ed / ESPEN Guidelines
clinicalPearls: Metabolic response to injury features an initial hypometabolic ebb phase followed by a hypercatabolic flow phase
Enteral nutrition is strongly preferred over parenteral nutrition to preserve gut mucosal integrity and prevent bacterial translocation
Refeeding syndrome causes life-threatening hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia upon rapid carbohydrate reintroduction
Caloric requirements in post-surgical patients average 25 to 30 kcal per kilogram per day with 1.5 to 2.0 g per kg protein
Immune-modulating enteral formulas enriched with arginine, glutamine, and omega-3 fatty acids improve outcomes in major surgical trauma
reference.pathophysiology: Tissue trauma, hemorrhage, and endotoxemia trigger afferent neural signals and release of proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6), stimulating the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and sympathoadrenal system. Cortisol, catecholamines, and glucagon surge while insulin sensitivity declines, inducing intense hepatic gluconeogenesis, skeletal muscle proteolysis, and lipolysis. In refeeding syndrome, sudden carbohydrate availability induces insulin secretion, driving phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells and precipitating acute ATP depletion, diaphragmatic weakness, and fatal cardiac arrhythmias.
additionalDifferentials: Adrenal insufficiency during acute surgical stress
additionalInvestigations: Serum electrolytes including phosphate, magnesium, and calcium before initiating nutritional support
Serum prealbumin and transferrin as dynamic markers of visceral protein synthesis
Twenty-four-hour urine urea nitrogen to calculate nitrogen balance
Blood glucose monitoring and arterial blood gas lactate levels
